info.bio:
Los Manfred mann fueron uno de los mejores grupos británicos de los 60's; un grupo que supo combinar muy bien su faceta R&B y jazz (la verdadera pasión de la banda), con el pop mas pegadizo y bien construido. 

La banda se forma en Londres a finales de 1962 con el nombre de The Mann-Hugg Blues Menn. Manfred Mann, cuyo nombre real era Manfred Lubowitz había nacido en Johanesburgo (Sudáfrica), pero en 1961 se fué de allí, principalmente por su descontento con el régimen de Apartheid que predominaba en su país.

scenes.name: Pop protesta y folk rock (1965)
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: El pop quería profundidad y el folk quería fama. En 1963 Dylan condensó el miedo atómico en «A Hard Rain’s a-Gonna Fall» y Peter, Paul and Mary llevaron «Blowin’ in the Wind» al número 2; en 1964 los Searchers demostraron que una letra sobre lluvia radiactiva («What Have They Done to the Rain») podía entrar en el Top 20. En 1965 Dylan triunfó en Inglaterra, Donovan arrasó con «Catch the Wind» y el «Mr Tambourine Man» de los Byrds abrió la veda: todos versionaban a Dylan y la «Pop Protest» amenazaba con ser una moda. «Eve of Destruction», de P. F. Sloan cantada por Barry McGuire y prohibida por la BBC, fue su cénit comercial y su nadir artístico. Tom Wilson, productor despedido por Dylan, añadió instrumentos eléctricos a la versión acústica de «The Sound of Silence» de Simon & Garfunkel, primer número 1 estadounidense de 1966 y señal de que el mercado de masas no temería la profundidad.

scenes.name: Beat, R&B y mod pop británico
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Tras el éxito de los Beatles, las cuatro grandes discográficas (EMI, Decca, Pye y Philips) saquearon metódicamente las provincias: firmaban barato y esperaban a ver qué pegaba. Pye, del veterano Louis Benjamin, tenía a los Kinks y a los Searchers y fama de contratos miserables. Los Ugly’s de Birmingham, nacidos del skiffle y curtidos en los clubes alemanes, se distinguían por su conciencia social; la cara B de su tercer single, «A Quiet Explosion» (21 de enero de 1966), con órgano Vox Continental, un riff con eco a lo Delia Derbyshire y un bajo descendente que es la bomba cayendo, desapareció en la sobreproducción del momento, pero es un disco extraño y auténtico que se acerca a la psicodelia. A principios de 1966 las bases del beat y del R&B se llevaron al límite, como bajo una enorme presión: «Keep on Running» de Spencer Davis casa soul y mod pop, los Wheels de Belfast aceleran sin freno en «Bad Little Woman» y los Poets de Glasgow, de Andrew Loog Oldham, desquician el «Baby Don’t You Do It» de Marvin Gaye.

scenes.name: El pop en televisión: Ready Steady Go! y Top of the Pops
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: A principios de 1966 había tres programas pop. Top of the Pops (BBC1) presentaba la lista tal cual, de Eddy Arnold a los Stones; A Whole Scene Going (BBC2), con Barry Fantoni y Wendy Varnals, era más reflexivo. El mejor era Ready Steady Go! (agosto de 1963-1966), que traducía al televisor el ritmo de la cultura juvenil: actuaciones en directo entre el público, mujeres como presentadoras, productoras y artistas (Vicki Wickham, Cathy McGowan), visitantes de Tamla y del soul, y la cámara de Michael Lindsay-Hogg pegada a Jagger y a las bailarinas mod de falda corta. En agosto de 1965 el público invadió el plató mientras los Stones tocaban «Satisfaction».

scenes.name: El fin del boom del beat británico
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Los Beatles habían empezado el ciclo a principios de 1963 y lo cerraron en septiembre de 1966. El ritmo implacable (tres singles al año, cientos de conciertos, fama mundial) pasó factura: crisis y hospitalizaciones (Jagger en junio, el aparente intento de suicidio de Scott Walker en agosto), Brian Jones desaparecido, Paul Jones dejó Manfred Mann, los Animals se rehicieron como New Animals, Georgie Fame disolvió los Blue Flames. La novela All Night Stand de Thom Keyes, un roman à clef sobre los Beatles, acaba con su estrella aburrida de sí misma. Sin el centro unificador de los Beatles volvió el entretenimiento ligero (los Bachelors, Ken Dodd y «Distant Drums» del difunto Jim Reeves, número 1 casi todo octubre), mientras en agosto la mitad del Top 50 británico era americana: Motown y los grupos de la Costa Oeste. «Una era ha terminado», escribió Chris Welch.

podcast.title: Formation as The Man Hugg Blues Brothers (1962)
podcast.body: Following Graham Bond's departure to form his own band, Manfred Mann (Lubawitz) and Mike Hugg decided to form their own group, combining their love for modern jazz with the more commercial R&B Bond was playing. The initial lineup included Mann on keyboards, Hugg on drums and vibraphone, Mac Vickers on guitar, flute, and saxophone, Dave Richmond on bass, Tony Roberts and Don Faye on saxophone, and Ian Fenby on trumpet. "They named their group the Man Hugg Blues Brothers, and it's initially consisted of Man on keyboards, Hugg and drums and vibraphone, Mac Vickers on guitar, flute and saxophone, Dave Richmond on bass, Tony Roberts and Don Faye on saxophone, and Ian Fenby on trumpet."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Name Change to Manfred Mann (1963)
podcast.body: Producer John Burgess, who signed the group to HMV Records, insisted they change their name from The Man Hugg Blues Brothers to "Manfred Mann." Paul Jones strongly disagreed, and even Manfred Mann himself found it "a little unreasonable," but the group eventually conceded, reassured that publicity would emphasize all five members were equal. The members themselves often referred to the group as "the Mann Fritz." "Burgess liked the group, but he insisted that they had to change their name, and in fact, he insisted that the group change their name to Manfred Mann."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Dave Richmond's Departure and Tom McGuinness's Arrival (1964)
podcast.body: Dave Richmond was seen as a "great jazz bass player" who wanted to emulate Charles Mingus, playing "strange cross-rhythms." The group needed someone to play "straightforward blues bass lines without complaint," closer to Willie Dixon. Tom McGuinness, a guitarist who bluffed his way into the bass player role, replaced Richmond. McGuinness had never played bass before his first gig and was only asked if he was willing to play simple parts during his interview. "Richmond was a great bass player, but he was a great jazz bass player. He wanted to be Charles Mingus, and play strange cross-vethams, and what the group needed at this point was someone who would just play straightforward blues bass lines without complaint, they needed someone closer to Willie Dixon than to Mingus."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Miserable American Tour (1964)
podcast.body: After the success of "Doo Wah Diddy Diddy," the group embarked on an American tour packaged with Peter and Gordon. The experience proved "thoroughly miserable," leading the group to decide against returning to the US, resulting in only minor successes there for the rest of the decade, despite continued hits in Britain. "The group found the experience of touring the US, a thoroughly miserable one, and decided that they weren't going to bother going back again."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Jack Bruce's Brief Tenure (1965)
podcast.body: To fill the bass vacancy, Jack Bruce was hired on Graham Bond's recommendation. Bruce had recently played with John Mayall's Bluesbreakers alongside Eric Clapton. He played bass on "Pretty Flamingo," which became the group's only UK number one. Bruce remained with the band for several months before leaving. "And its Bruce who played bass on the group's next big hit, Fitty Flamingo. The only UK number one the vues ever played on."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Klaus Voormann Joins (1965)
podcast.body: After Jack Bruce's departure, Klaus Voormann replaced him on bass. Voormann was an old friend of The Beatles from their Hamburg days, having been taught the basics of bass by Stuart Sutcliffe, and had formed the trio Paddy, Klaus and Gibson. Like Vickers, Voormann could play the flute, and his flute playing became a regular feature on later singles. "Verman was an old friend of the Beatles from their Hamburg days, who had been taught the rudiments of bass by Stuart Sukliff, and had formed a trio, Paddy Klaus in Gibson, with two merzy-beam musicians, Paddy Chambers of the Big Three, and Gibson Camp of King's Highest Tale of the Dominoes."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Mike Vickers' Departure (1965)
podcast.body: Mike Vickers left the group to pursue a career in arranging film music and session work. His later projects included work for The Beatles, the music for the 1972 film "Dracula A.D.," and the opening and closing themes for "This Week in Baseball." "Mike Vickers, who went off to work in arranging film music and session work, including some work for The Beatles, the music for the film Dracula A.D. in 1972, and the opening and closing themes for this week in baseball."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Paul Jones' Growing Annoyance (1965)
podcast.body: Paul Jones became increasingly frustrated that despite being the frontman, lead singer, cover picker, and writer of much original material, records were credited to the group's keyboard player, Manfred Mann. "Jones was getting increasingly annoyed at the fact that the record the group was making were hit, and he was the frontman, the lead singer, the person picking the cover versions, and the writer of much of the original material, but all the records were getting credited to the group's keyboard player."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Tom McGuinness Switches to Guitar (1965)
podcast.body: Following Mike Vickers' departure, Tom McGuinness took the opportunity to switch from bass to guitar, his preferred instrument. "The Maganis took the opportunity of Vickers leaving the group to switch from bass back to playing guitar, which had always been his preferred instrument."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Mike Davo Joins (1966)
podcast.body: Mike Davo, formerly lead singer of A Band of Angels, eventually replaced Paul Jones. Jones himself unknowingly suggested Davo as a possible replacement, unaware he was already chosen. Manfred Mann recounted a silent drive to their last gig with Jones, where Dylan's "Just Like a Woman," their first single with Davo, played on the radio, highlighting the discomfort within the band. "Jones actually mentioned Davo to his bandmates as a possible replacement, not realising he was already in the group."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Paul Jones' Departure (1966)
podcast.body: Paul Jones announced his intention to quit the group concurrently with Mike Vickers' departure, but was persuaded to stay for nearly a year while a replacement was sought. Auditions with singers like Rod Stewart and Long John Baldry were unsuccessful. Relations between Jones and the rest of the group deteriorated to the point where they didn't inform him they were considering Mike Davo as his replacement. "But by the time that track was released, Paul Jones was out of the group. He actually announced his intention to quit the group at the same time that Mike Vickers left, but the group had persuaded him to stay on for almost a year while they looked for his replacement, or auditioning singers like Rudge Stewart and Long John Bouldery with little success."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Record Label Split and Career Concerns (1966)
podcast.body: When Paul Jones left, the band faced a difficult situation as their record label decided to keep Jones as a solo performer. The rest of the group had to find another label and feared their career was over without Jones. "There was a lot of discomfort in the band at this time, because their record label had decided to stick with Jones as a solo performer, and the rest of the group had had to find another label, and were worried that without Jones their career was over."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Members' Post-Split Careers (1969 onwards)
podcast.body: After the split, Mike Davo appeared on the original "Jesus Christ Superstar" album and became known for writing advertising jingles, notably "A finger of fudge is just enough for Cadbury's." Tom McGuinness formed McGuinness Flint, having a hit with "When I'm Dead and Gone," and later reunited with Paul Jones to form The Blues Band. Paul Jones became a born-again Christian in the 80s, starred in the children's TV show "Uncle Jack," and hosted the BBC Radio 2 Blues program for 32 years. Manfred Mann and Mike Hugg formed Manfred Mann Chapter Three, releasing two albums. Hugg then wrote theme music for TV and films, including "Whatever Happened to the Likely Lads." Manfred Mann went on to form Manfred Mann's Earth Band, having hits like Bruce Springsteen's "Blinded By The Light." "The groups split up in 1969 and went their separate ways. Dabo appeared on the original Jesus Christ Superstar album, and then went into writing advertising jingles."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Split in 1969
podcast.body: By January 1969, Tom McGuinness stated, "It's not a group anymore, it's just five people who come together to make hit singles. That's the only aim of the group at the moment, to make hit singles, it's the only reason the group exists." The group formally split later that year. "The groups split up in 1969 and went their separate ways."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: "No A-Sides by Group Members" Rule
podcast.body: During Mike Davo's tenure as lead singer, the group operated under an implicit "no A-sides by group members" rule, which limited their material choices. Davo himself was a songwriter and wrote two hit singles, "Handbags and Glad Rags" and "Build Me Up Buttercup," that the group never recorded. "Dabo was himself a songwriter, and it shows the limitations of the No A sides by group members rule. The wild Dabo was the lead singer of Manfred Mann, he wrote two hit singles which the group never recorded."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Biographical Portrayal Contrast
podcast.body: The narrative highlights that biographies on Manfred Man's lead singers do not feature the same misogynistic and critical tone found in some writings about Diana Ross, suggesting a double standard in how male and female artists are portrayed. "Oddly, the books I'm using for the upcoming episodes on Manfred Man and the Beach Boys don't talk of their lead singers in this way."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Eclectic Catalogue and Critical Reassessment
podcast.body: Manfred Mann was a band with too many musical interests for a coherent image, and their reliance on outside songwriters and frequent lineup changes meant they lacked a consistent sound compared to contemporaries. However, this eclecticism created a catalog that "rewards exploration" and may warrant a major critical reassessment in the future. "Manfred Mann were a band with too many musical interests to have a coherent image, and their alliance and outside songwriters, and their frequent lineup changes, meant that they never had the consistent sound of many of their contemporaries."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Mike Vickers' Later Career
podcast.body: After his time with Manfred Mann and session work, Mike Vickers now spends his time creating experimental animations. "Mike Vickers now spends his time creating experimental animations."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Musical Direction Shift and Horn Section Departure
podcast.body: With Paul Jones joining as lead singer and harmonica player after auditioning at the Crawdaddy Club called The Rolling Twenties, the group's musical direction shifted to Chicago Blues, popular at The Marquee Club, where they secured a residency. This contrasted with the soul style expected from a horn-centric lineup at the nearby Flamingo Club, leading to the horn players (Tony Roberts, Don Faye, Ian Fenby) leaving, solidifying the group as a five-piece core of Jones, Mann, Hugg, Vickers, and Richmond. "Unsurprisingly, given this, the horn players soon left, and the group became a five-piece core of Jones, Mann, Hugg, Vickers, and Richmond."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Search for a Blues Singer
podcast.body: As their experiences leaned more towards jazz, the group sought a singer more familiar with the blues. They chose Paul Pund, who had been friends with Brian Jones of The Rolling Stones and had adopted Jones's surname, performing as Paul Jones. "As their experiences were far more in the jazz field than in blues, they decided that they needed to get in a singer who was more familiar with the blues side of things."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: The Manfreds Reunion (1990s)
podcast.body: Almost uniquely for an early 60s band, all members of the classic Manfred Mann lineup were still alive. Hugg, Jones, McGuinness, and Davo reunited as The Manfreds in the 1990s, with Mike Vickers also joining until 1999, and continue to tour. Manfred Mann continues to perform with his Earth Band. "Hugg, Jones, McGuinness and Davo reunited as the Manfreds in the 1990s, with Vickers also in the band until 1999, and continued to tour together."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

xref.title: Joining Rush
xref.body: Neil Peart formally became a member of Rush on July 29th, 1974, a date which coincided with Geddy Lee's 21st birthday. He secured the position after auditioning, replacing founding drummer John Rutsey. His first gig with the band was shortly after, on August 14th, 1974, in Pittsburgh, where Rush opened for Uriah Heep and Manfred Mann. "He got the job and formally became a member of Rush on July 29th, 1974, which just happened to be Gettie Lee's 21st birthday."
